question: Which statement best describes Title & meta description?
options: <link rel="canonical"> tells search engines the 'official' URL for a page when the same content is reachable via multiple URLs (tracking params, http/https, trailing slashes, print versions). It consolidates ranking signals onto one URL and prevents duplicate-content dilution. It should point to an absolute URL.

Twitter/X uses its own twitter: tags to build a card. twitter:card chooses the layout ('summary' or 'summary_large_image'), and twitter:title/description/image set the content. X falls back to Open Graph when twitter tags are missing, so many sites set OG tags plus just twitter:card.

Open Graph (og:) tags control how a URL renders when shared on Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, and most chat apps. The four essentials are og:title, og:description, og:image (1200×630 recommended), and og:url; og:type ('website', 'article') classifies the content. Without them, platforms guess from the page and previews look broken.

The <title> is the single most important on-page SEO signal: it shows as the clickable headline in search results and the browser tab. The <meta name="description"> is the snippet shown under that headline — it isn't a ranking factor, but a compelling, unique 120–160 character description improves click-through. Both should be unique per page.

question: Which statement best describes Open Graph tags?
options: <meta name="robots"> controls how crawlers index a specific page. 'noindex' keeps the page out of search results; 'nofollow' tells crawlers not to follow its links. Common values combine them, e.g. 'noindex, nofollow' for thank-you or admin pages. This is page-level control, distinct from the site-wide robots.txt file.
